course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions

topic.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
topic.summary: Zeros and factors, multiplicity, conjugate pairs of non-real zeros, finding degree from differences, and even and odd symmetry.

lesson.title: Polynomial Functions and Complex Zeros
lesson.summary: Zeros and factors, multiplicity, conjugate pairs of non-real zeros, finding degree from differences, and even and odd symmetry.
learningGoals: Connect real zeros, linear factors, and x-intercepts, and use zeros to solve polynomial inequalities.
Describe how multiplicity affects the graph at a zero, and count complex zeros using the degree.
Find a polynomial's degree from successive differences and decide whether a function is even, odd, or neither.
lesson.bigIdea: A polynomial's zeros, with their multiplicities, are its fingerprints. They determine its factors, where its graph crosses or touches the x-axis, and how many complex zeros it has.
lesson.context: Topic 1.4 showed that zeros and turning points are linked. Here zeros take center stage. You will work with real zeros that appear as x-intercepts and with non-real zeros that never appear on the graph but still count toward the degree.

sections.title: A real zero corresponds to a linear factor.

blocks.text: A number a is a zero of a polynomial p when p(a) = 0. For a real number a, the expression (x − a) is a factor of p exactly when a is a zero. Real zeros are also the x-intercepts of the graph. For example, p(x) = x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 factors as (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3), so its zeros are 1, −2, and 3.
Real zeros also split the number line into intervals where the polynomial keeps one sign. To solve p(x) > 0, find the zeros, then test one input in each interval between them.

blocks.caption: Sign of p(x) = (x − 1)(x + 2)(x − 3) between its zeros

blocks.text: So p(x) > 0 on the intervals (−2, 1) and (3, ∞). The zeros are the boundaries between positive and negative stretches.

sections.takeaway: Zeros give factors, x-intercepts, and the boundaries of the intervals where a polynomial is positive or negative.

sections.title: A repeated factor gives a zero with multiplicity.

blocks.text: If the factor (x − a) appears n times, then a is a zero of multiplicity n. A polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex zeros when each zero is counted as many times as its multiplicity. For p(x) = (x + 1)²(x − 2)³, the zero −1 has multiplicity 2, the zero 2 has multiplicity 3, and the degree is 5.

blocks.caption: Multiplicity and the graph for p(x) = (x + 1)²(x − 2)³
rows: Touches the x-axis and turns around; the output keeps the same sign on both sides
Crosses the x-axis; the output changes sign

blocks.text: A real zero of even multiplicity does not change the sign of the output, so the graph touches the x-axis there. A real zero of odd multiplicity does change the sign, so the graph passes through the x-axis.

sections.takeaway: Even multiplicity means touch and turn. Odd multiplicity means cross.

sections.title: Non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs.

blocks.text: A complex number has the form a + bi, where a and b are real and i² = −1. When a polynomial has real coefficients, its non-real zeros come in conjugate pairs: if a + bi is a zero with b ≠ 0, then a − bi is a zero too. For instance, x² + 4 has zeros 2i and −2i, and x² − 2x + 5 has zeros 1 + 2i and 1 − 2i.

Non-real zeros never appear as x-intercepts, but they still count toward the degree. Because they come in pairs, a real-coefficient polynomial of odd degree always has at least one real zero. The polynomial (x² + 4)(x − 1) has degree 3 and three complex zeros, 2i, −2i, and 1, but its graph meets the x-axis only once.

sections.takeaway: Non-real zeros pair up as conjugates, so they can reduce the number of x-intercepts without changing the degree.

sections.title: Successive differences reveal the degree from a table.

blocks.text: When outputs are given at equally spaced inputs, take differences between consecutive outputs, then differences of those differences, and so on. The degree of the polynomial is the smallest n for which the nth differences are constant.

blocks.caption: Successive differences for outputs of x³ at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5

blocks.text: The third differences are the first constant row, so the degree is 3. This works only when the inputs are equally spaced.

sections.takeaway: The degree is the number of times you must take differences before they become constant.

sections.title: Even and odd functions have symmetry.

blocks.text: A function f is an even function if f(−x) = f(x) for every x in its domain. Its graph is symmetric about the y-axis, and power functions with even exponents, such as x² and x⁴, are even. A function f is an odd function if f(−x) = −f(x). Its graph is symmetric about the origin, and power functions with odd exponents, such as x and x³, are odd.

blocks.caption: Testing symmetry
rows: −x³ + x², neither the same nor the opposite

sections.takeaway: Replace x with −x. The same function means even, the opposite means odd, and anything else means neither.

vocabulary.definition: The number of times a factor (x − a) appears in a polynomial, which is the multiplicity of the zero a.
A number of the form a + bi, where a and b are real numbers and i² = −1.
Two complex numbers a + bi and a − bi that differ only in the sign of the imaginary part.
Differences between consecutive outputs, then differences of those differences, and so on, taken at equally spaced inputs.
A function with f(−x) = f(x) for every x in its domain, so its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
A function with f(−x) = −f(x) for every x in its domain, so its graph is symmetric about the origin.

connections.title: Turning points sit between zeros
connections.body: Topic 1.4 showed there is at least one turning point between two distinct real zeros. Multiplicity adds a twist: at a zero of even multiplicity the graph itself turns around right on the x-axis.
connections.transferQuestion: How does a double zero relate to a local extremum?
connections.feedback: At a zero of even multiplicity the graph touches the axis and turns, so that zero is also a local maximum or minimum.

connections.title: Zeros will help with rational functions
connections.body: In Topics 1.8 through 1.10 the zeros of numerators and denominators decide where rational functions cross, approach, or skip the x-axis. Multiplicity reappears there when you compare numerator and denominator factors.
connections.transferQuestion: If a factor appears in both a numerator and a denominator, what do you expect to happen at that input?
connections.feedback: Expect something special to happen there. Topic 1.10 shows it can create a hole in the graph.
